breaths.text: Ruan Steyn woke in a Long Street garret that charged rent like a personal insult and watched Table Mountain through warped glass as if the mountain were a jury that declined to speak.
He had an article in him about extraordinary men and the right to step over blood for a higher arithmetic.
Alida the pawnbroker sat in his mind as a louse with keys.
Erik Roux climbed the stairs with bread and friendship; Steyn smiled wrong and sent him away.
Cape Town’s Sea Point glass flashed far off like a visa his soul could not afford.
He pawned a watch, counted her building’s steps, and felt theory trying on a body.
Later the same necessity continued without becoming a different book: garret thickened instead of forking.
Steyn’s face learned new ways to hide; Sonja’s learned new ways to wait; Inspector Vos’s learned new ways to smile.
Long Street kept its noise.
The garret kept its insult.
The axe, gone from hands, stayed in nights.
Dostoevsky’s pressure—idea, blood, mother, sister, detective, saint, suicide, confession, dust—remained the only engine.
Cape Town supplied mountain, harbor, and glamorous glass as cooler surfaces, not as excuses.
In a tavern he overheard talk of Alida’s cruelty and felt destiny wink—ideas recruit that way.
He drank little.
Clarity, he told himself, was his gift.
He saw Sonja Marais’s future before he knew her name, through her father’s drunk confessions: a daughter selling herself for bread, icons in a poor room, suffering as another ledger.
He gave money he could not spare and hated the gift for making him feel chosen.
Later the same necessity continued without becoming a different book: tavern recruit thickened instead of forking.

He took the axe from a shed and killed Alida.
Liesel entered with a bundle and became the second death his article had not budgeted.
Blood made philosophy smell like a room.
He washed badly, hid goods, fainted into fever.
Soft-invention refused him cleverness; Dostoevsky’s crime stayed stupid and heavy.
The mountain watched.
Police farce and chance delayed him.
Guilt did not.

He left money again.

He knelt incompletely while people laughed.

Cape Town supplied mountain, harbor, and glamorous glass as cooler surfaces, not as excuses.
Steyn reread his article on extraordinary men until the words looked like alibis.
Long Street noise entered the garret as if to mock abstraction.
He underlined a sentence about stepping over and felt the underline as a rehearsal.
Erik Roux, had he seen it, would have argued him into bread and work.
He hid the pages.
At Alida’s he pawned a ring and mapped the room: icons, chest, door, Liesel’s possible entrance.
Mapping felt like scholarship.
Scholarship was how he avoided the word murder.
She insulted him with a price.
The insult entered the article as evidence.
After the murders he walked toward the harbor without seeing cranes.
A street preacher spoke of sin; Steyn laughed and the laugh became a file in Inspector Vos’s future.
He threw evidence into water that did not care.
Water’s indifference was not absolution.
Paula touched his face and forgave him for thinness she could see.
She could not see the axe.
Dina saw more and said less.
Lukas Louw’s bouquet smelled like ownership.
Steyn’s anger at Lukas Louw was the cleanest feeling he had left.
Sonja’s icon corner held a light that did not flatter.
She told him God saw.
He told her God was a rumor for the weak.
She did not argue; she waited.
Waiting undid him more than argument.
Inspector Vos’s smile said: I can wait longer than your pride.
Steyn’s pride said: watch me.
Pride lost on points over weeks.
The mountain outside shifted shadow like a slow gavel.
Dina’s gun in Sarel Visser’s room did not fire and still ended a plotline.
She walked out unbroken enough to break him.
He released her because even predators sometimes recognize a wall.
Dawn near the harbor finished him without needing Steyn’s axe.
The clerk’s boredom cracked when confession arrived in ordinary language.
Ordinary language is Dostoevsky’s preferred blade.
Sonja waited outside.
Erik Roux shook.
The mountain was not visible from the station’s inner room; Steyn felt its absence like a missing witness.
The road inland removed Table Mountain from his eye and left the idea alone with him.
Sonja’s visits were logistics and love.
He dreamed plague-ideas eating cities.
When he took her hand without contempt, the article finally lost a reader.
Cape Town reseated the fever.
Theory, axe, guilt, Inspector Vos, Sonja, dust—beats held.
Sensibility held.
